newsitem.title: ITALY: Skeleton Italy budget seen buoying positive market.
newsitem.headline: Skeleton Italy budget seen buoying positive market.

text.p: Italy's government is set to sketch out a 1998 budget which is weighted heavily towards spending cuts, and economists say the measures should add buoyancy to already optimistic financial markets.
A Treasury official said last week Italy would need 25
trillion lire of deficit-cutting measures next year to meet key European monetary union criteria and newspapers have since reported details of what they say are plans for the package.
Based on those reports, economists expect around 17 trillion lire of spending cuts and eight trillion lire of higher revenue.
The broad outline of the budget will emerge when the government presents a three-year economic plan next week.

Gregorio De Felice, head of research at Banca Commerciale Italiana here, said if the budget looked like the kind of package outlined in newspapers -- with structural cuts in state spending --- then financial markets would be happy.

"The spread between BTPs and Bunds would fall further. There is potentially more room for a rise in prices, so there will be a fall in yields, if market expectations on the structural character of the measure is confirmed, " De Felice said.

Italian government bonds (BTPs) and the lira are already buoyant due to growing expectations the Bank of Italy may cut its 6.75 percent discount rate in the next few days ,providing preliminary inflation data due on Tuesday and Wednesday comes in as low as 1.5 percent year-on-year as the market expects.

The gap between yields on the 10-year BTP and the benchmark 10-year Bund narrowed to a record 136 basis points in early trading and the lira is at 982 per mark, close to its highest levels against the German currency since mid-February.
Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas in London, said the
market was on a firm footing at the moment because sentiment was very positive about prospects for Italy's interest rates, public finances and European economic and monetary union (EMU).

"Overall given current feeling in the market its response to a package of this kind would probably be positive even though there are doubts about the welfare reform programme and hitting the deficit target in 1997 and 1998," Wattret said.
The centre-left government is under pressure from
doubting European partners to cut structural spending in order to pare its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product -- enough to join and stay in EMU from its January 1999 start.
Its three-year plan (Dpef), which will signal the
numerical targets for meeting EMU criteria, is due to be examined by the cabinet next week, later than had originally been expected.
The government is treading a fine line between drafting a
plan which wins over EU partners but retains key parliamentary support of its hard-left allies the Communist Refoundation party, which is adamantly opposed to cuts in state spending.
"If the Dpef has these structural contents, if there is
an agreement between the government and Refoundation, the Btp-Bund spread could fall to 100-120 basis points," De Felice said.
However Lorenzo Codogno at Bank of America said the
package as outlined by newspapers is not out of line with forecasts and its presentation is unlikely to boost markets much although the Btp-Bund spread could narrow 10 basis points.
But economists see plenty of scope for market weakness
once debate gets underway this summer between the government, trade unions and the hard left on exactly where to cut spending for the final budget draft due in September.
Codogno said the Btp-Bund spread could splay temporarily
to 180 or even 200 over the summer if political debate was fierce, while the lira could drop temporarily beyond 1,000 per mark.
